CHAPTER XVII

THE MUSOLINE OVERTURE


Mrs. Adair, on her side, asked for no explanations. She was naturally,
behind her pale and placid countenance, a woman of a tortuous and
intriguing mind. She preferred to look through a keyhole even when she
could walk straight in at the door; and knowledge which could be gained
by a little maneuvering was always more desirable and precious in her
eyes than any information which a simple question would elicit. She
avoided, indeed, the direct question on a perverted sort of principle,
and she thought a day very well spent if at the close of it she had
outwitted a companion into telling her spontaneously some trivial and
unimportant piece of news which a straightforward request would have at
once secured for her at breakfast-time.

Therefore, though she was mystified by the little white feather upon
which Ethne seemed to set so much store, and wondered at the good news
of Harry Feversham which Captain Willoughby had brought, and vainly
puzzled her brains in conjecture as to what in the world could have
happened on that night at Ramelton so many years ago, she betrayed
nothing whatever of her perplexity all through lunch; on the contrary,
she plied her guest with conversation upon indifferent topics. Mrs.
Adair could be good company when she chose, and she chose now. But it
was not to any purpose.

"I don't believe that you hear a single word I am saying!" she
exclaimed.

Ethne laughed and pleaded guilty. She betook herself to her room as soon
as lunch was finished, and allowed herself an afternoon of solitude.
Sitting at her window, she repeated slowly the story which Willoughby
had told to her that morning, and her heart thrilled to it as to music
divinely played. The regret that he had not come home and told it a year
ago, when she was free, was a small thing in comparison with the story
itself. It could not outweigh the great gladness which that brought to
her--it had, indeed, completely vanished from her thoughts. Her pride,
which had never recovered from the blow which Harry Feversham had dealt
to her in the hall at Lennon House, was now quite restored, and by the
man who had dealt the blow. She was aglow with it, and most grateful to
Harry Feversham for that he had, at so much peril to himself, restored
it. She was conscious of a new exhilaration in the sunlight, of a
quicker pulsation in her blood. Her youth was given back to her upon
that August afternoon.

Ethne unlocked a drawer in her dressing-case, and took from it the
portrait which alone of all Harry Feversham's presents she had kept. She
rejoiced that she had kept it. It was the portrait of some one who was
dead to her--that she knew very well, for there was no thought of
disloyalty toward Durrance in her breast--but the some one was a friend.
She looked at it with a great happiness and contentment, because Harry
Feversham had needed no expression of faith from her to inspire him,
and no encouragement from her to keep him through the years on the level
of his high inspiration. When she put it back again, she laid the white
feather in the drawer with it and locked the two things up together.

She came back to her window. Out upon the lawn a light breeze made the
shadows from the high trees dance, the sunlight mellowed and reddened.
But Ethne was of her county, as Harry Feversham had long ago discovered,
and her heart yearned for it at this moment. It was the month of August.
The first of the heather would be out upon the hillsides of Donegal, and
she wished that the good news had been brought to her there. The regret
that it had not was her crumpled rose-leaf. Here she was in a strange
land; there the brown mountains, with their outcroppings of granite and
the voices of the streams, would have shared, she almost thought, in her
new happiness. Great sorrows or great joys had this in common for Ethne
Eustace, they both drew her homewards, since there endurance was more
easy and gladness more complete.

She had, however, one living tie with Donegal at her side, for Dermod's
old collie dog had become her inseparable companion. To him she made her
confidence, and if at times her voice broke in tears, why, the dog would
not tell. She came to understand much which Willoughby had omitted, and
which Feversham had never told. Those three years of concealment in the
small and crowded city of Suakin, for instance, with the troops marching
out to battle, and returning dust-strewn and bleeding and laurelled with
victory. Harry Feversham had to slink away at their approach, lest some
old friend of his--Durrance, perhaps, or Willoughby, or Trench--should
notice him and penetrate his disguise. The panic which had beset him
when first he saw the dark brown walls of Berber, the night in the
ruined acres, the stumbling search for the well amongst the shifting
sandhills of Obak,--Ethne had vivid pictures of these incidents, and as
she thought of each she asked herself: "Where was I then? What was I
doing?"

She sat in a golden mist until the lights began to change upon the still
water of the creek, and the rooks wheeled noisily out from the tree-tops
to sort themselves for the night, and warned her of evening.

She brought to the dinner-table that night a buoyancy of spirit which
surprised her companions. Mrs. Adair had to admit that seldom had her
eyes shone so starrily, or the colour so freshly graced her cheeks. She
was more than ever certain that Captain Willoughby had brought stirring
news; she was more than ever tortured by her vain efforts to guess its
nature. But Mrs. Adair, in spite of her perplexities, took her share in
the talk, and that dinner passed with a freedom from embarrassment
unknown since Durrance had come home to Guessens. For he, too, threw off
a burden of restraint; his spirits rose to match Ethne's; he answered
laugh with laugh, and from his face that habitual look of tension, the
look of a man listening with all his might that his ears might make good
the loss of his eyes, passed altogether away.

"You will play on your violin to-night, I think," he said with a smile,
as they rose from the table.

"Yes," she answered, "I will--with all my heart."

Durrance laughed and held open the door. The violin had remained locked
in its case during these last two months. Durrance had come to look upon
that violin as a gauge and test. If the world was going well with Ethne,
the case was unlocked, the instrument was allowed to speak; if the world
went ill, it was kept silent lest it should say too much, and open old
wounds and lay them bare to other eyes. Ethne herself knew it for an
indiscreet friend. But it was to be brought out to-night.

Mrs. Adair lingered until Ethne was out of ear-shot.

"You have noticed the change in her to-night?" she said.

"Yes. Have I not?" answered Durrance. "One has waited for it, hoped for
it, despaired of it."

"Are you so glad of the change?"

Durrance threw back his head. "Do you wonder that I am glad? Kind,
friendly, unselfish--these things she has always been. But there is more
than friendliness evident to-night, and for the first time it's
evident."

There came a look of pity upon Mrs. Adair's face, and she passed out of
the room without another word. Durrance took all of that great change in
Ethne to himself. Mrs. Adair drew up the blinds of the drawing-room,
opened the window, and let the moonlight in; and then, as she saw Ethne
unlocking the case of her violin, she went out on to the terrace. She
felt that she could not sit patiently in her company. So that when
Durrance entered the drawing-room he found Ethne alone there. She was
seated in the window, and already tightening the strings of her violin.
Durrance took a chair behind her in the shadows.

"What shall I play to you?" she asked.

"The Musoline Overture," he answered. "You played it on the first
evening when I came to Ramelton. I remember so well how you played it
then. Play it again to-night. I want to compare."

"I have played it since."

"Never to me."

They were alone in the room; the windows stood open; it was a night of
moonlight. Ethne suddenly crossed to the lamp and put it out. She
resumed her seat, while Durrance remained in the shadow, leaning
forward, with his hands upon his knees, listening--but with an
intentness of which he had given no sign that evening. He was applying,
as he thought, a final test upon which his life and hers should be
decided. Ethne's violin would tell him assuredly whether he was right or
no. Would friendship speak from it or the something more than
friendship?

Ethne played the overture, and as she played she forgot that Durrance
was in the room behind her. In the garden the air was still and
summer-warm and fragrant; on the creek the moonlight lay like a solid
floor of silver; the trees stood dreaming to the stars; and as the music
floated loud out across the silent lawn, Ethne had a sudden fancy that
it might perhaps travel down the creek and over Salcombe Bar and across
the moonlit seas, and strike small yet wonderfully clear like fairy
music upon the ears of a man sleeping somewhere far away beneath the
brightness of the southern stars with the cool night wind of the desert
blowing upon his face.

"If he could only hear!" she thought. "If he could only wake and know
that what he heard was a message of friendship!"

And with this fancy in her mind she played with such skill as she had
never used before; she made of her violin a voice of sympathy. The fancy
grew and changed as she played. The music became a bridge swung in
mid-air across the world, upon which just for these few minutes she and
Harry Feversham might meet and shake hands. They would separate, of
course, forthwith, and each one go upon the allotted way. But these few
minutes would be a help to both along the separate ways. The chords rang
upon silence. It seemed to Ethne that they declaimed the pride which had
come to her that day. Her fancy grew into a belief. It was no longer "If
he should hear," but "He _must_ hear!" And so carried away was she from
the discretion of thought that a strange hope suddenly sprang up and
enthralled her.

"If he could answer!"

She lingered upon the last bars, waiting for the answer; and when the
music had died down to silence, she sat with her violin upon her knees,
looking eagerly out across the moonlit garden.

And an answer did come, but it was not carried up the creek and across
the lawn. It came from the dark shadows of the room behind her, and it
was spoken through the voice of Durrance.

"Ethne, where do you think I heard that overture last played?"

Ethne was roused with a start to the consciousness that Durrance was in
the room, and she answered like one shaken suddenly out of sleep.

"Why, you told me. At Ramelton, when you first came to Lennon House."

"I have heard it since, though it was not played by you. It was not
really played at all. But a melody of it and not even that really, but a
suggestion of a melody, I heard stumbled out upon a zither, with many
false notes, by a Greek in a bare little whitewashed café, lit by one
glaring lamp, at Wadi Halfa."

"This overture?" she said. "How strange!"

"Not so strange after all. For the Greek was Harry Feversham."

So the answer had come. Ethne had no doubt that it was an answer. She
sat very still in the moonlight; only had any one bent over her with
eyes to see, he would have discovered that her eyelids were closed.
There followed a long silence. She did not consider why Durrance, having
kept this knowledge secret so long, should speak of it now. She did not
ask what Harry Feversham was doing that he must play the zither in a
mean café at Wadi Halfa. But it seemed to her that he had spoken to her
as she to him. The music had, after all, been a bridge. It was not even
strange that he had used Durrance's voice wherewith to speak to her.

"When was this?" she asked at length.

"In February of this year. I will tell you about it."

"Yes, please, tell me."

And Durrance spoke out of the shadows of the room.

All through luncheon, though the small white feather in Ethne’s possession prickled her curiosity like a burr caught in lace, though Captain Willoughby’s tidings about Harry Feversham set her thoughts tapping and turning, though the old night at Ramelton—years ago now—hovered at the edge of her guesses like a name half-forgotten in a dying dialect, she showed no sign. She poured out talk on indifferent things with practiced brightness.

It did no good.

“I don’t believe you hear a single word I am saying!” she broke out at last.

Ethne laughed, and admitted it as frankly as if she had been caught seasoning a dish absent-mindedly while someone read aloud a menu.

As soon as luncheon was done she escaped to her room and claimed the afternoon for solitude. From her window the estate lay mild and orderly, yet her thoughts ran far from it, running and returning like a tune that will not let itself be translated into speech. She repeated, slowly, the story Willoughby had brought her in the morning, and it went through her like music played with the right pressure and the right pause—thrilling not because it argued, but because it sounded true.

The small regret—that he had not come home and told it a year ago, when she had been free—was there, but it lay light, like a crumpled rose-leaf under a mattress that could not ruin sleep. The story itself overwhelmed it. Harry Feversham, who had struck the blow at Lennon House, had also, at peril to himself, restored the pride that blow had broken. It was a strange restitution: the hand that had shamed her had, without asking her faith or permission, laboured to give her back her own regard. Gratitude warmed her with a quickening like sunlight on skin after long cloud. Youth, which she had thought spent, came back on that August afternoon in the way a lost taste returns suddenly to the tongue.

She unlocked a drawer in her dressing-case and took out the one portrait—of all his gifts—the only one she had kept. She was clear with herself. The man in the picture was dead to her in the only way that mattered; there was no thought of disloyalty towards Durrance. Yet the dead may still be friends. She looked at the likeness with contentment not sharpened by longing, but softened by respect. He had needed no encouragement from her to keep him on the level of a hard inspiration. When she put the portrait away, she laid the little white feather beside it, as if sealing together two tokens whose meanings could not be rendered into any plain, dominant vocabulary, and locked the drawer.

She returned to the window.

A light breeze made the shadows of the high trees dance in broken patterns over the lawn. The sun mellowed and reddened; the creek beyond held the sky’s colour as a pan holds a slow-browned glaze. Yet, for all the richness of the scene, her heart tugged homewards. She was of her county—Harry Feversham had found that out long ago—and great sorrow and great joy drew her alike to Donegal, where endurance came easier and gladness felt complete. It was August: the first heather would be out on the hillsides, and she could almost smell it, a dry sweetness over peat and granite. She wished the news had found her there, among the brown mountains and the voices of streams that spoke an older language than any drawing-room ever managed. Here, in this strange land, she could not help feeling that even happiness had a different accent.

But Donegal was not wholly absent. Dermod’s old collie had become her shadow; his warm, patient presence was a kind of hearth. To him she spoke her confidence, and if her voice broke, he would never carry the tale beyond her knees. With him at her feet she filled in, from Willoughby’s omissions and from what Feversham had never told, the missing parts as one reconstructs a vanished recipe from scent and texture. Those three years of concealment in Suakin, for instance: the small crowded streets, the troops marching out and coming back dust-stained, bleeding, crowned with victory. She saw Feversham slipping away at their approach, his whole body tuned to danger, afraid an old friend—Durrance, perhaps, or Willoughby, or Trench—might catch a familiar movement and pierce a disguise. She saw the first panic when Berber’s dark brown walls rose ahead; the night in the ruined acres; the stumbling search for the well among Obak’s shifting sandhills. Each picture came with its own taste of fear—metal on the tongue, sand in the throat—and with each she asked, not as a reproach but as a startled accounting, Where was I then? What was I doing?

She sat in that golden drift of thought until the light changed on the creek, until rooks wheeled noisily from the treetops to settle themselves for the night, their calls stitching the evening together. The sound drew her back as surely as a bell recalls a cook from the far end of the market.

At dinner she brought a buoyancy that startled her companions. Mrs. Adair, peering sideways as ever, had to admit that seldom had Ethne’s eyes shone so starrily, or colour sat so freshly on her cheeks. She grew more certain that Willoughby’s news had been of the stirring sort; she grew more tortured by her failure to name it. Yet the meal passed with an ease they had not known since Durrance’s return to Guessens. He, too, threw off some restraint. His spirits rose to meet Ethne’s; he answered laugh with laugh, and that habitual tension—the look of a man listening with his whole life, making his ears stand in for lost eyes—fell away from his face for once, as if the house’s soundscape had softened enough to let him rest inside it.

“You will play on your violin to-night, I think,” he said when they rose.

“Yes,” she answered, “I will—with all my heart.”

He laughed and held the door.

The violin had stayed locked in its case these last two months. Durrance had come to treat that case like a gauge. When the world went well with Ethne, the lid opened and the instrument was allowed to speak; when it went ill, it stayed shut, lest it say too much, lay open old wounds, and expose them to eyes that had no right. Ethne herself knew it for an indiscreet friend—like some cherished dish that reveals, by its very aroma, what has been happening in the kitchen.

But to-night it would be brought out.

Mrs. Adair lingered until Ethne was out of earshot.

“You have noticed the change in her to-night?” she asked.

“Yes. Have I not?” Durrance replied.

“One has waited for it, hoped for it, despaired of it.”

“Are you so glad of the change?”

Durrance tipped his head back.

“Do you wonder that I am glad? Kind, friendly, unselfish—these things she has always been. But there is more than friendliness evident to-night, and for the first time it’s evident.”

A look of pity crossed Mrs. Adair’s face. She went out without another word.

Durrance took all of that change to himself.

Mrs. Adair, restless as a kettle just before boiling, drew up the blinds in the drawing-room, opened the window, and admitted the moonlight. Then, seeing Ethne unlocking the violin-case, she stepped out onto the terrace; she could not sit patiently in the room and watch a secret unfold without her.

So when Durrance entered the drawing-room, he found Ethne alone. She sat in the window, already tightening the strings, turning each peg with the careful, exact ear of someone who understands that a world can be made unbearable by the wrong pitch. Outside, the night’s sounds lay clear: the faint lap from the creek, a distant insect’s steady rasp, leaves shifting with the smallest wind. No harsh machinery intruded; no bought entertainment shouted over the quiet. The house held an older peace, the sort modern noise tries to sell back to people in bottles.

Durrance took a chair behind her in the shadows.

“What shall I play to you?” she asked.

“The Musoline Overture,” he said. “You played it on the first evening when I came to Ramelton. I remember how you played it then. Play it again to-night. I want to compare.”

“I have played it since.”

“Never to me.”

They were alone. The windows stood open on moonlight. Ethne rose suddenly, crossed to the lamp, and put it out. The room deepened; the moon became their only light. She returned to her seat. Durrance remained behind her, leaning forward, hands on his knees, listening—not with the relaxed pleasure he had shown at dinner, but with an intentness he had hidden, like a man tasting for a secret ingredient.

He was making, as he believed, a final test on which his life and hers should turn. The violin would tell him what words could not. Would it speak only friendship—or the thing beyond friendship?

Ethne began the overture, and as soon as the bow drew its first clear line of sound, she forgot he was there.

The garden lay still, warm with summer; scent rose from the borders, thick and sweet as if crushed leaves had been rubbed between fingers. The creek held the moonlight like a solid floor of silver. Trees stood dreaming up at the stars. The music floated out over the lawn into the clean, attentive night, and with it a fancy took her—swift, irrational, irresistible—that the sound might travel down the creek, over Salcombe Bar, and across the bright seas until it struck, small but piercingly clear like fairy music, on the ears of a man sleeping far away under southern stars, the cool desert wind on his face.

If he could only hear, she thought. If he could only wake and know it was a message of friendship.

And with that in her mind she played with a skill she had never used before, not for display but for meaning. She made the violin a voice of sympathy, as if tenderness could be tuned and carried.

The fancy grew as the overture unfolded. The music became a bridge swung in mid-air across the world, and for a few minutes she and Harry Feversham might meet upon it and clasp hands. They would part at once, each returning to the path allotted—yet those minutes would strengthen both to continue.

The chords rang out into silence, and it seemed to her they declared the pride that had returned to her that day. Her fancy hardened into belief. It was no longer If he should hear; it was He must hear. And then, swept past caution, a strange hope sprang up and took her whole attention:

If he could answer.

She lingered on the last bars, holding them as one holds back the final taste of a dish, waiting for the moment after when the mouth understands what it has been given. When the music died, she sat with the violin across her knees and stared out across the moonlit garden, listening for an impossible reply.

An answer came.

Not from the creek, not across the lawn, not from any distance that could be crossed by wind and water.

It came from the dark behind her, spoken in Durrance’s voice.

“Ethne, where do you think I heard that overture last played?”

She started, as if shaken awake.

“Why—you told me. At Ramelton, when you first came to Lennon House.”

“I have heard it since,” he said. “Though it was not played by you. It was not really played at all. But a melody of it—and not even that really, but a suggestion of a melody—I heard stumbled out on a zither, with many false notes, by a Greek in a bare little whitewashed café, lit by one glaring lamp, at Wadi Halfa.”

“This overture?” she whispered. “How strange!”

“Not so strange after all. For the Greek was Harry Feversham.”

So the answer had come.

Ethne sat very still in the moonlight. Anyone bending close might have seen her eyelids closed, as if she were trying to keep the moment intact against the bluntness of sight. A long silence followed. She did not ask why Durrance, having kept such knowledge for so long, chose to speak of it now. She did not ask what had driven Harry Feversham to scrape at a zither in a mean café at Wadi Halfa. The details did not yet want naming; the experience felt untranslatable, like some private dialect of the heart that would only be damaged by forcing it into common words.

It seemed to her simply that he had spoken to her as she had played to him. The music, after all, had been a bridge. It did not even feel strange that he had used Durrance’s voice.

“When was this?” she asked at last.

“In February of this year. I will tell you about it.”

“Yes,” she said. “Please, tell me.”

And Durrance, out of the shadows, began to speak.
